doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

chapter: Singing in England and moving to North America
title: Singing with postwar British bands and early repertoire
summary: Postwar revival bands gave her chances to sing; she lists tunes like Baby Doll and Young Woman Blues and making other songs fit Bessie's idiom.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: So did you need to search out other musicians a few years later, so that you could get to sing?

No because suddenly, don’t forget this was getting into the late 40s, and just after the war, and we were starting to have these bands sprouting up, all having listened to records and not always the best records because we had this rose thorn don’t forget that took a lot away from the fidelity, and so everybody was mad to play like all of these bands that they had heard. So there was a lot of opportunity to sing around with mostly university students who subsequently either went on to become doctors, lawyers or indeed some of them, like Monty Sunshine or Chris Barber, Ken Collier, did form bands and did become quite successful, very successful in the jazz business in England.
Do you recall some of the first tunes that you sang with these bands?

Well of course I sang “Ice Cream,” I sang “Baby Doll,” which is very sophisticated, Bessie Smith’s “Baby Doll,” “Young Woman Blues,” “Careless Love Blues,” “Alexander’s Ragtime Band” with the verse because that was so marvelous. I think there was a mistake on the original recording and they never cleared it up and I always thought that was fascinating. And then I sang a lot of things that really didn’t seem related to jazz but I felt that there was a possibility of making them in the idiom, which I still do with Bob. I take a song that I’ve heard that you can make it sound like Bessie could have sung it if she’d have known. I mean for instance, Bud Freeman once told us that he heard Bessie singing “I’ll See You In My Dreams.” And apparently, you think about this,

[sings] See you in my dreams, you know, it would have worked. And apparently according to Chris Albertson, who wrote the definitive book on Bessie, that she sang “Smoke Gets In Your Eyes,” and I don’t doubt it because people were required to sing all kinds of material.
Well that gives a whole different spin to the lyrics of “I’ll See You In My Dreams” to see it like that.

Yes it does. But I think that you can, if you think about all the great songs that there’s a way of hearing them and thinking. Bob has always said if Benny [Goodman] didn’t play this he should have done it.
